open-question.question: A Claude Code `gurita` marketplace registered from the Settings window carries, as its ref, the tag of the release that was latest when it was installed, so `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and `claude plugin update gurita@gurita` keep reading that tag. Once a newer release is published, how does an update from the window bring the marketplace registration, at each scope it stands at, to the newer release's tag?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: It moves exactly the declarations paired with the copies being updated, through the harness's own CLI and the scopes the check already prints, whereas moving every declared scope needs a declaration's scope, which `claude plugin marketplace list --json` does not give, and the other options either write Claude Code's files from outside or replace the recorded scoped `claude plugin update` with a reinstall.
open-question.alternative: Mechanism: the update re-runs `claude plugin marketplace add --scope <scope>` with the new tag's source over the existing `gurita` declaration, removing nothing. Scopes moved: only the scopes the update targets, those at which a Gurita copy applying to the open project was detected, each declaration there moved to the new tag; any `gurita` declaration at another scope stays as it stands. Then `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and the scoped `claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s <scope>` per detected scope, in the one run. The registrations moved are exactly the ones paired with the copies being updated, matching the marketplace registration scope decision's one-declaration-per-install-scope pairing, so an update touches no settings file the person's copies do not depend on. It carries the same unobserved dependence on `marketplace add` overwriting a same-name declaration, and a declaration left on the old tag at a scope with no detected copy (a user-scope one from an earlier manual add, for example) may be the one Claude Code resolves the `gurita` name to, so a scoped update could still read the old tag; how Claude Code picks among same-name declarations at several scopes is unobserved.

Mechanism: the update re-runs `claude plugin marketplace add --scope <scope>` on `uHappyLogic/gurita-claude` with a source carrying the newly read tag, over the existing `gurita` declaration, which nothing removes first. Scopes moved: every scope at which a `gurita` marketplace declaration applying to the open project stands (user settings, the project's `.claude/settings.json`, the project's local settings), whether or not a Gurita copy was detected there. Then, in the same run, `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and one `claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s <scope>` per detected copy's scope, as the update target scopes decision lists them. Only the harness's own documented CLI touches the registration and no copy is uninstalled, and because no declaration of the name is left on the old tag, no stale registration at another scope can shadow the moved one or keep serving the old release to the scoped update. It depends on `marketplace add` replacing an existing same-name declaration's source rather than refusing or ignoring it, which no one has observed (whether it does so is for the hands-on verification sibling to establish). It also moves a declaration no detected copy uses, such as a user-scope one that serves copies in other projects, and rewrites the tracked `.claude/settings.json` of a project whose copy stands only at another scope.

Mechanism: at each scope at which a Gurita copy applying to the open project was detected, the update runs `claude plugin marketplace remove gurita --scope <scope>`, then `claude plugin marketplace add --scope <scope>` with the new tag's source, then `claude plugin install gurita@gurita --scope <scope>`, so an update of Claude Code is a reinstall at each detected scope rather than a call to `claude plugin update`. Scopes moved: the detected copies' scopes only, since removing a declaration that serves copies elsewhere would take those copies with it; declarations at other scopes stay as they stand. It relies on no unobserved overwrite behaviour: removal and a fresh add are each the documented way to change a marketplace's source, so after the run each moved registration carries the new tag whatever `marketplace add` does to an existing name. Removing a marketplace may uninstall the plugins installed from it and drop their enabled state, so a failure between the removal and the reinstall leaves the harness with no Gurita copy at that scope; the update also stops being an update in Claude Code's own terms, and a disabled copy's state or its configuration may not survive the reinstall.

alternative.id: Rewrite ref at every declared scope

open-question.alternative: Mechanism: the extension itself rewrites the ref carried by the `gurita` marketplace declaration in the settings file of each scope where one applying to the open project stands (the user-scope marketplace record, the project's `.claude/settings.json`, the project's local settings), changing that field alone and running no marketplace add or remove. Scopes moved: every declared scope, whether or not a copy was detected there. Then `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and the scoped `claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s <scope>` per detected scope, in the one run. The change is exactly one field per declaration, under the extension's own control and independent of how the CLI treats a repeated add, and no copy is uninstalled or left stale at any scope. It writes Claude Code's own settings and its internal marketplace record from outside the harness, against the goal's "by that harness's own install path", tying the extension to file formats Claude Code may change and that no CLI help documents, and it moves declarations no detected copy uses, the tracked `.claude/settings.json` included.

alternative.id: Rewrite ref at detected scopes only

open-question.alternative: Mechanism: the extension rewrites the ref field of the `gurita` marketplace declaration in the settings file of each scope at which a Gurita copy applying to the open project was detected, and of no other, running no marketplace add or remove; declarations at other scopes stay as they stand. Then `claude plugin marketplace update gurita` and the scoped `claude plugin update gurita@gurita -s <scope>` per detected scope, in the one run. It is the narrowest change: one field in each settings file paired with a copy being updated, with no reliance on the CLI's handling of a repeated add and no uninstall. It carries the same direct writes into Claude Code's own files, outside the harness's own install path, plus the risk that a same-name declaration left on the old tag at another scope is the one the scoped update resolves to.

open-question.question: Codex has no plugin update command, and `codex plugin marketplace upgrade` only refreshes the snapshot of the ref a marketplace was registered with, which for an install made from the Settings window is one release's tag. Which commands make up an update of the Codex Gurita copy to a newer release's tag?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Removing and re-adding the registration leaves it at the new tag whatever `marketplace add` does to a name already configured, every command is one the CLI's help lists, and the update never uninstalls the plugin, so a failed step leaves the working copy in place rather than no copy at all.
open-question.alternative: The update moves the marketplace registration to the newer tag by removing it and adding it again, and then installs the plugin again over the copy still standing: `codex plugin marketplace remove gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>` (or `uHappyLogic/gurita-codex@<tag>`), then `codex plugin add gurita@gurita`, run in that order in one run, each behind the previous one's success. The installed plugin is never removed by the update itself. Every command is one the Codex CLI documents (`marketplace remove` and `add` with `--ref` both appear in its help text), the registration ends exactly as a fresh install from the window would leave it, at the newer tag, and the plugin is never deliberately uninstalled, so the copy stays in place if a later step fails. Whether `marketplace remove` leaves an installed plugin of that marketplace installed, orphaned, or uninstalled, and whether `plugin add` over an installed copy replaces it with the new version, is unobserved; a failure between the remove and the add leaves Codex with no `gurita` marketplace registered, and the old version's directory under `~/.codex/plugins/cache/gurita/gurita/` may stay behind beside the new one.

The update uninstalls the copy and its registration and installs both again at the newer tag: `codex plugin remove gurita@gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace remove gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>`, then `codex plugin add gurita@gurita`, in that order in one run, each behind the previous one's success. It relies on no unobserved behaviour of a command run over existing state: every step acts on a known starting point, the old version's cache is removed by `plugin remove` as its help text states, and the end state is identical to a first install from the window. It is the longest sequence and the one that leaves Codex with no Gurita copy at all for the duration, so a failure after the first step (a network fault during `marketplace add`, for example) ends with the plugin uninstalled; it also discards whatever Codex recorded about the copy beyond its presence, such as its enabled state, and uses an uninstall command inside a window whose goal adds no uninstall control.

The update runs exactly the install's two commands again with the newer tag, removing nothing: `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>` over the already registered `gurita` marketplace, then `codex plugin add gurita@gurita`. Install and update share one command sequence and differ only in the tag read. It is the shortest sequence, one code path serves both Install and Update, and nothing is ever removed, so no failure can leave Codex with less than it had before the click. Whether `marketplace add` on a name already configured replaces its ref, refuses as a duplicate, or adds a second entry is unobserved and undocumented in the help text; if it refuses, the update cannot work at all, and if it silently keeps the old ref, the update reports success while the copy stays at the old release.

The update moves the marketplace registration to the newer tag by removing it and adding it again (`codex plugin marketplace remove gurita`, then `codex plugin marketplace add uHappyLogic/gurita-codex --ref <tag>`) and runs no `codex plugin add`, leaving Codex to take the newer version from the refreshed marketplace snapshot for the copy already installed. It touches the installed plugin with no command at all, so the copy's install record and enabled state are never rewritten and the run is two commands. The installed copy stands in a version-keyed directory (`~/.codex/plugins/cache/gurita/gurita/<version>/`), which suggests that only an install writes a new version's files, so the update may end with the marketplace at the new tag and the plugin still at the old version; nothing observed so far shows Codex moving an installed copy to a newer snapshot by itself.

The update rewrites the ref of the `gurita` marketplace entry in `~/.codex/config.toml` to the newer tag, the extension writing that file itself, then runs `codex plugin marketplace upgrade gurita` to refresh the snapshot at the new ref and `codex plugin add gurita@gurita` to install the new version from it. It uses the one refresh command Codex offers for its intended purpose and changes nothing about the registration but its ref, with no window in which the marketplace is unregistered. The extension would write a configuration file Codex owns, whose layout for marketplace entries is neither documented in the CLI help nor stable across Codex releases, which departs from the goal's install by the harness's own install path and breaks silently when Codex changes that layout.
